# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–29 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Spring of eighth year after Waterloo, continuing into summer**. Year is 1830 (French Revolution occurred this year). John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Dispersal from Pumpernickel**: Continental tour continuing; Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Becky now established at **Ostend** (seaside resort, fashionable summer destination for watering-place society).
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms (hill farms where Amelia and Georgy summer retreat); Bryngate (market town); Pumpernickel (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss, Aurelius Platz, Zwieback's Conditorey, Saint Michael's Fountain, Artillery Place, Stadthaus, Town Hall, Redoute, gardens); Elephant lodging-house (Room No. 90/92); **Ostend** (seaport, German resort; Dr. von Glauber's preferred destination; now Amelia's party lodged in "exceedingly dear and uncomfortable house"); Chatham (Dobbin joined --th regiment); various other Continental locations previously established.

## Rebecca's Seduction of Jos and Integration into Household (Chapters 27–28)

**Gaming and Initial Seduction**: At Pumpernickel Stadthaus gaming, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon), formerly with Rawdon Crawley, encountered Jos. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Through manipulation—hiding degradation evidence, offering tender looks, claiming heart first learned to beat at his presence—convinced Jos she was virtuous and wronged.

**Becky's True Nature**: After Jos left, revealed true character to Max and Fritz (Schoppenhausen students). Mimicked Jos while eating and drinking brandy-and-water. Bohemian nature inherited from parents. Had falsely advertised Leipzig concert; won money at trente-et-quarante using young Georgy as player; planned to spend winnings on wine and theatre rather than respectability.

**Dobbin's Opposition and Jos's Resentment**: Jos confided affecting history to Major Dobbin (omitting gaming). Dobbin called her "the little minx," mistrusted her, recalled Rawdon was "confounded blackleg" who cheated George, remembered scandal about separation. Jos resented Dobbin's superiority. Stormy colloquy ended by Becky's arrival with meagre baggage.

**Amelia's Embrace; Dobbin's Departure**: Becky greeted Jos affectionately; made shrinking salutation to Dobbin, whom she recognized as enemy. Amelia embraced Becky warmly, flung Dobbin "an angry look—the most unjust and scornful glance" of her life. Had private reasons for anger. Dobbin departed with haughty bow. **FACT: Dobbin had spent fifteen years devoted to Amelia; she had grown accustomed to trampling on him but did not wish to marry him—only to keep him.**

**Becky's False Narrative**: Claimed child "torn from her arms shrieking" by Rawdon's cruelty. Gave full version: marriage viewed with hostility; sister-in-law poisoned husband's mind; bore poverty and neglect; driven to demand separation when Rawdon asked her sacrifice fair fame for advancement through Marquis of Steyne. Forced to flee; Rawdon took child in revenge. Emmy cried, offered Becky her own room, insisted she stay.

**Household Manipulation**: Within week, Jos became "sworn slave and frantic admirer"—drove with Becky publicly, invented festivities. Becky discovered how to soothe Emmy: praised Dobbin constantly, told Emmy she had behaved cruelly toward him. Made Georgy write constantly to Major, sent "Mamma's kind love." Amelia's maid initially disliked Becky for dismissing Dobbin; reconciled when Becky became his "most ardent admirer."

**Becky's Reformation Appearance**: On arrival claimed baggage left at Leipzig (suspiciously); Emmy supplied clothes from own stores, took her to best milliner. No more torn collars or faded silks. Becky changed habits—rouge-pot suspended, spirit-and-water indulged only privately when Jos offered. Courier Kirsch indulged in Cognac; Becky "did not very likely indulge so much as she used before."

**Boxes Arrived; Miniature Obtained**: Much-bragged-about boxes from Leipzig arrived—three not large or splendid; Becky took no dresses or ornaments from them. From papers box, she took picture with great glee: gentleman in pencil, face painted pink, riding on elephant from Eastern scene—Jos's miniature. Jos delighted; Emmy only came in very tired and unwell; Jos and Becky had "charming tete-a-tete," Rebecca singing old songs of 1815 to him.

**Amelia's Regret and Awareness**: Emmy made aware of Dobbin's movements through Georgy's continued correspondence. William wrote once or twice "in a manner so unconstrainedly cold" that Amelia "felt now in her turn that she had lost her power over him." He was free. "He had left her, and she was wretched." Memory of his countless services and lofty affectionate regard rebuked her day and night. She brooded, reproached herself for "having flung away such a treasure."

**Dobbin's Career Advancement**: Jos read that Major Dobbin joined --th regiment at Chatham. Subsequently read announcements of presentations of Colonel Sir Michael O'Dowd, K.C.B., and Lady O'Dowd, Miss Glorvina O'Dowd. Dobbin's name appeared among Lieutenant-Colonels: old Marshal Tiptoff died during passage from Madras; Sovereign advanced Colonel Sir Michael O'Dowd to Major-General on return to England with indication he should be Colonel of distinguished regiment.

**Summer Walks and Conversations at Coldcombe**: During summer evenings at hill farms, Emmy and Georgy took long walks (Rebecca left with Jos). Mother told son Major William was "best man in all the world--the gentlest and the kindest, the bravest and the humblest." Reminded Georgy they owed everything to Dobbin's benevolent care; how he befriended them through poverty, watched over them when nobody cared, how all comrades admired him. Told Georgy his father trusted William above all men; that William had defended young George at school against a tyrant; friendship never ceased until George's death.

**Dobbin's Final Speech and Rejection**: William told Amelia: "It is not that speech of yesterday which moves you...I have loved you and watched you for fifteen years in vain. Have I not learned in that time to read all your feelings? I know what your heart is capable of: it can cling faithfully to a recollection and cherish a fancy, but it can't feel such an attachment as mine deserves...You are not worthy of the love which I have devoted to you...I will bargain no more: I withdraw...Good-bye, Amelia! We are both weary of it." He broke the chain by which she held him. Left with "head on his breast"; never looked back as carriage passed under Amelia's window. Georgy left in street "burst out crying."

**Amelia's Treasuring of Dobbin**: Emmy cleared away Dobbin's books (German dictionary with "William Dobbin, --th Reg.," guide-book with initials) and stored them on drawers with her work-box, desk, Bible, prayer-book under pictures of two Georges. Dobbin left gloves behind; Georgy later found them neatly folded in secret-drawers of mother's desk.

## Chapter 29 – Ostend and Crisis (Summer)

**Persuasion to Ostend**: Doctor von Glauber (Court Doctor at Pumpernickel) persuaded Jos—calling him "regular milch-cow"—that both he and his "charming sister" (Emmy) needed summer at Ostend. Emmy indifferent to location. Georgy jumped at move. Becky came "as a matter of course in the fourth place inside of the fine barouche Mr. Jos had bought." She had misgivings about friends whom she might meet at Ostend who could tell "ugly stories," but believed herself "strong enough to hold her own." She had cast "such an anchor in Jos...as would require a strong storm to shake. That incident of the picture had finished him." Becky took down her elephant miniature, put it into little box which she had "from Amelia ever so many years ago." Emmy came with her "Lares--her two pictures" (of two Georges). Party finally lodged in "exceedingly dear and uncomfortable house at Ostend."

**Ostend Society and Snubbing**: Amelia began to take baths. Scores of Becky's acquaintances passed her and cut her, yet Mrs. Osborne, who walked about with her and "knew nobody, was not aware of the treatment experienced by the friend whom she had chosen." Becky never thought fit to tell her.

**Disreputable Acquaintances**: Among Becky's acquaintances who acknowledged her were Major Loder (unattached) and Captain Rook (late of the Rifles), who might be seen smoking on the Dike. They "speedily got an introduction to the hospitable board and select circle of Mr. Joseph Sedley. In fact they would take no denial; they burst into the house whether Becky was at home or not, walked into Mrs. Osborne's drawing-room, which they perfumed with their coats and mustachios, called Jos 'Old buck,' and invaded his dinner-table, and laughed and drank for long hours there."

**Amelia's Distress**: Emmy inspired with "intolerable terror and aversion" by their presence. They paid her "tipsy compliments"; they leered at her over dinner-table. Captain made "advances that filled her with sickening dismay"; she would never see him unless George was by her side. Both men had designs upon her—"A couple of ruffians were fighting for this innocent creature, gambling for her at her own table."

**Amelia's Secret Letter**: "At last she took a great resolution--made the great plunge. She wrote off a letter to a friend whom she had on the other side of the water, a letter about which she did not speak a word to anybody, which she carried herself to the post under her shawl." When Georgy met her, she looked "very much flushed and agitated"; kissed and hung over him greatly that night. Did not come out of her room after return. Becky thought Major Loder and Captain frightened her.

**Becky's Intervention and Cruelty**: Becky reasoned: "She must go away, the silly little fool. She is still whimpering after that gaby of a husband--dead (and served right!) these fifteen years. She shan't marry either of these men...She shall marry the bamboo cane, I'll settle it this very night."

Becky marched up and down room before Amelia, "surveying her with a sort of contemptuous kindness": "You must go away from here and from the impertinences of these men. I won't have you harassed by them...Jos can't protect you...You must marry, or you and your precious boy will go to ruin. You must have a husband, you fool; and one of the best gentlemen I ever saw has offered you a hundred times, and you have rejected him, you silly, heartless, ungrateful little creature!"

**Becky's Revelations About George**: "Couldn't forget HIM!" cried Becky, describing George Osborne as "that selfish humbug, that low-bred cockney dandy, that padded booby, who had neither wit, nor manners, nor heart, and was no more to be compared to your friend with the bamboo cane than you are to Queen Elizabeth. Why, the man was weary of you, and would have jilted you, but that Dobbin forced him to keep his word. He owned it to me. He never cared for you. He used to sneer about you to me, time after time, and made love to me the week after he married you."

**The Letter and Amelia's Collapse**: Becky took paper from her belt, opened it, flung it into Emmy's lap: "You know his handwriting. He wrote that to me--wanted me to run away with him--gave it me under your nose, the day before he was shot--and served him right!"

**Emmy's Tears and Revelation**: Emmy's head sank; "for almost the last time in which she shall be called upon to weep in this history, she commenced that work. Her head fell to her bosom, and her hands went up to her eyes; and there for a while, she gave way to her emotions, as Becky stood on and regarded her." Internal analysis: "Was she most grieved because the idol of her life was tumbled down and shivered at her feet, or indignant that her love had been so despised, or glad because the barrier was removed which modesty had placed between her and a new, a real affection? 'There is nothing to forbid me now,' she thought. 'I may love him with all my heart now. Oh, I will, I will, if he will but let me and forgive me.' I believe it was this feeling rushed over all the others which agitated that gentle little bosom."

**KEY FACT ABOUT GEORGE**: **George Osborne was faithless and contemptuous; made love to Becky week after marrying Amelia; Dobbin forced him to keep his word to Amelia; Becky possesses written evidence (letter where George wanted to run away with her, given under Amelia's nose day before Waterloo).**

## Character States (End of Chapter 29)
- **Amelia**: Suffers revelation of George's infidelity and contempt; idol shattered; barrier to loving Dobbin removed; believes she may now love him "with all my heart" if he will "let me and forgive me"; emotionally devastated and transformed.
- **Major Dobbin**: Departed Pumpernickel; promoted to Lieutenant-Colonel; advanced through O'Dowd's elevation; wrote coldly to Amelia, asserting freedom; maintains correspondence with Georgy only.
- **Rebecca**: Integrated into household; enslaved Jos through miniature; manipulates Amelia; maintains reformed appearance; now at Ostend; possesses George's letter; cruel architect of Amelia's revelation; unchanged in fundamental nature.
- **Jos Sedley**: Enslaved to Becky; "regular milch-cow" to Doctor; weak, cannot protect anyone.
- **Georgy**: Correspondent with Dobbin; influenced by mother's praise of Dobbin; friendly with Becky.
